pronunciation.notes: All has one syllable and one common pronunciation in each variety; unlike a, an, and the, it is not reduced to a weak form in ordinary speech.

core_idea: All points to the complete amount or number of something, with nothing left out.

senses.definition: used before a noun to mean the complete amount, number, or group, with no part left out
senses.explanation: All goes directly before a plural or uncountable noun (all children, all water) or before the, a possessive, or a demonstrative and then a noun (all the students, all my money, all those books). All of is also possible before these: all of the students.

examples.text: All children need love and attention.
She spent all her money on the trip.
All the seats in the theater were full.

senses.definition: used before a noun of time or place to mean the whole of it, from beginning to end or from one side to the other
senses.explanation: This use is common with day, night, week, and way: it rained all day; we walked all the way home.

examples.text: It rained all day, so we stayed inside.
Mari studied all night before the exam.
The road was blocked all the way to the bridge.
We waited all week for the package to arrive.

phrases.definition: used after a negative, in a question, or after if, to mean in any way or to any degree
phrases.explanation: It adds emphasis and is not used in an ordinary positive statement.

examples.text: I don't like it at all.
Do you know him at all?
If you have any doubts at all, tell me now.

adaptation.grammar: At all strengthens a negative or a question and cannot stand in an ordinary positive statement: I don't like it at all, but not I like it at all.

phrases.definition: used to give your opinion after considering everything

examples.text: The trip had a few problems, but all in all it was a success.
All in all, I'm happy with how things turned out.

synonym_discrimination.note: All and every both mean every single one, but every takes a singular noun and a singular verb (every child knows), while all takes a plural or uncountable noun (all children know, all the water is gone). Whole means complete, with no part missing, and goes with a singular noun after a or the: the whole cake. All the cake is also possible, but whole is more usual for one single thing.

usage_note: All can also stand alone as a pronoun, meaning everything or everyone: that is all; all are welcome. Before a personal pronoun object, all follows it rather than coming before it: I ate it all (or all of it, all of them), not I ate all it.

learner_errors.incorrect: All of students like the teacher.
learner_errors.correct: All of the students like the teacher.
learner_errors.note: All of needs the, a possessive, or a pronoun after it; without of, no article is needed: all students.

learner_errors.incorrect: All my two sisters live abroad.
learner_errors.note: For exactly two people or things, both is used, not all.

adaptation.semantic: All can mean the whole of one thing (all the money) or every member of a group (all the students); some languages use two different words for these.
adaptation.grammar: Before a noun that already has the, a possessive, or a demonstrative, all comes first and needs no of: all the students, all my money. Before a plain plural or uncountable noun, all is used with no article: all children, all water.
